first part, the exercise itself. This
exercise is called the soleus pump, and
it targets a single small muscle in the
back of your leg called, you guessed it,
the soleus muscle. Here's how to do it.
Sit in a chair with your heels planted
on the floor. You want to lift your toes
and the front of your foot up and then
lower them back down repeatedly at a
steady pace. That's it. That's the whole
thing. No equipment, no standing up, and
no having to leave your desk or even the
table. This exercise was studied
specifically because the soleus muscle
behaves differently from almost every
other muscle in your body. Most muscles
rely heavily on stored glycogen for fuel
during light activity, meaning they burn
their own internal fuel reserves before
pulling sugar from your blood. The
soleus muscle does the opposite. Because
of its unique fiber type and unusually
high blood supply, it prefers to pull
glucose directly from your bloodstream
continuously for as long as it stays
active rather than relying mainly on its
own stored fuel. This means that
activating the soleus muscle right after
you're done eating, when all of the food
floods your bloodstream full of glucose,
that glucose from the blood will
literally get sucked up by the soleus
muscle, and therefore you need less
insulin to clear the same amount of
blood glucose. If your insulin stays
lower as much as possible, this leads to
a higher degree of insulin sensitivity.
